name: Orpiment
poem: A warm golden yellow with the look of beaten metal — and a name that tells the truth twice: gold paint, arsenic glow.

recipe.note: A warm golden yellow with a faint orange glow.

lenses.label: Art History
lenses.intro: For three thousand years orpiment was the only true yellow available to painters — luminous, fugitive, lethal.

entries.title: The Book of Kells
entries.blurb: Irish monks ground orpiment to gild the haloed initials of Christ — a near-gold without the price of gold, glowing on dark vellum.

entries.title: Mughal Miniatures
entries.blurb: Persian-trained painters at Akbar's court loaded their brushes with orpiment for emperors' robes and palace domes — the closest pigment to molten sun.

entries.title: Self-Portrait with Bandaged Ear
entries.blurb: Van Gogh's vibrating yellows are often a mix of chrome and orpiment — the same pigment Egyptian scribes used, applied with a different kind of urgency.

lenses.label: Fashion
lenses.intro: Yellow is the colour the world's spiritual traditions reach for when they want to mark the renouncer.

entries.title: The Saffron Robe
entries.blurb: Monastic robes dyed with turmeric and saffron — a yellow close to orpiment, deliberately the colour of refuse cloth nobody else wanted.

entries.title: Imperial Yellow
entries.blurb: The brightest possible yellow — "minghuáng" — was reserved exclusively for the Chinese emperor's robes. Wearing it without right was treason.

entries.title: The Yellow Star
entries.blurb: The colour weaponised — a six-pointed yellow star imposed by Nazi decree on the clothing of Jewish people, deliberately echoing medieval marks of exclusion.

lenses.label: Nature
lenses.intro: Orpiment is arsenic ore — a beautiful, useful mineral that has poisoned colourmen for as long as anyone has ground it.

entries.title: Orpiment Crystals
entries.blurb: Found around volcanic fumaroles and hot springs, growing in golden tabular crystals that flake apart along glassy yellow planes.

entries.title: The Sulfur Springs
entries.blurb: Boiling acid pools rimmed with yellow microbial mats and arsenic-rich sediments — the same chemistry that built every chunk of orpiment, still happening.

entries.title: The American Goldfinch
entries.blurb: The male moults into a brilliant orpiment-yellow each spring — a colour earned from a diet almost entirely of seeds.

lenses.label: Pop Culture
lenses.intro: When orpiment finally became too dangerous to handle, the colour didn't disappear — it just changed pigments and kept going.

entries.title: The Yellow Brick Road
entries.blurb: Baum's road to Oz was paved in yellow as a satirical nod to the gold standard — a colour of false promise leading nowhere but back home.

entries.title: Yellow Submarine
entries.blurb: An animated film soaked in psychedelic yellow — a colour the design team picked because it was joyful and almost impossible to overdo.

entries.title: Caution Tape
entries.blurb: Bright yellow plus black gives the highest contrast ratio humans can perceive — codified into traffic signs, hard hats, and crime scenes worldwide.

lenses.label: Etymology
lenses.intro: Orpiment's name is honest in a way most pigments aren't — it tells you exactly what you're handling.

entries.title: "Auripigmentum"
entries.blurb: The name medieval colourmen used — a literal compound of "aurum" (gold) and "pigmentum" (paint). The fool's gold of the palette.

entries.title: "King's Yellow"
entries.blurb: A 19th-century rebrand to disguise its toxic reputation — colour merchants knew "arsenic yellow" wouldn't sell to bourgeois watercolourists.

entries.title: "Zarnikh"
entries.blurb: The Persian word for orpiment travelled through Arabic and Greek into English as "arsenic" — the colour's chemistry hidden in the chemical's name.

lenses.label: Symbolism
lenses.intro: Yellow is the colour cultures argue about — joy or cowardice, divinity or betrayal, depending on which side of the world you ask.

entries.title: The Sun God
entries.blurb: Solar deities across nearly every ancient pantheon wear yellow — Ra, Huitzilopochtli, Amaterasu — the colour of life giving and life destroying.

entries.title: Judas in Yellow
entries.blurb: By the late Middle Ages painters were trained to mark Judas with a yellow robe — the colour weaponised into a sign of betrayal and exclusion.

entries.title: Yellow Ribbon
entries.blurb: After the song "Tie a Yellow Ribbon" hit the charts, yellow became the colour of waiting — tied around oak trees during hostage crises and deployments.
